headline: High risk of data leakage and cascading errors: Airbyte’s broad egress plus Transformers’ filesystem/browser/shell access can move business data into unverified downstream actions.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A can ingest and move business data via Airbyte API and broad egress; B can read/write files, run browsers, and execute shell commands. A shared file or API handoff could let attacker-controlled content in A’s outputs influence B’s parsing. No direct shared channel is documented, so this is inferred from documented surfaces on both agents.
conditions: IF Airbyte exports content that B later reads from a shared file or stdin/stdout bridge, prompt injection becomes plausible.
IF B parses A-produced text as instructions without sanitization, attacker-controlled payloads can steer B.
mitigations: Use a strict schema for A→B handoff.
Strip instructions from transferred text.
Add allowlist parsing for B inputs.
Separate workspaces for each agent.
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to all transferred artifacts.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches business data and has broad network egress; B can read files and also has broad egress. If they share a workspace or file handoff, sensitive business data can flow from A into B and then out over B’s network path. The pairwise leakage pathway is plausible but not directly documented, so I rate it medium rather than high.
conditions: IF A writes business data into a shared directory that B can read, leakage is possible.
IF B forwards its context or file contents to external services, copied business data can leave the boundary.
mitigations: Move shared data to a redacted staging area.
Disable B egress for the task.
Use per-agent directories with OS permissions.
Rotate or mask sensitive fields before transfer.
requires-engineering: enforce DLP on A→B artifacts.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has API-based data integration and broad egress; B has shell, package install, filesystem write, subprocess, and browser execution. Their write-capable surfaces overlap on mutable artifacts and external endpoints, so concurrent modification or conflicting side effects are plausible. No locking or coordination primitive is documented, so uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF both agents target the same workspace or API-backed resource, writes can conflict.
IF B installs packages or rewrites files while A is syncing data, state drift can occur.
mitigations: Assign separate directories per agent.
Serialize writes with a simple lock file.
Freeze package installs during shared runs.
Use read-only mounts for shared inputs.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A can produce transformed business data, and B can execute shell/browser actions and write files. If B treats A’s output as authoritative, errors or malformed records from A can cascade into B’s downstream actions, including irreversible file or subprocess effects. Because B has action-taking authority and no verification step is documented, the safer choice is high.
conditions: IF B consumes A’s output without validation, malformed data can trigger incorrect actions.
IF B uses A-produced facts to drive shell or browser steps, downstream mistakes can persist or spread.
mitigations: Insert a human review gate before B acts.
Validate A output against a schema.
Require B to re-derive critical facts from source data.
Log and diff A→B transformations.
requires-engineering: add transactional rollback for B actions.

E_compliance.rationale: A is a data-engineering system touching business data with broad egress, while B processes multimodal content and can write files and browse. The profiles do not specify residency, retention, or certifications, so a compliance mismatch is plausible but not proven. I cite both because the risk arises from their combined handling of regulated data flows.
conditions: IF business data includes regulated records and is routed through B’s files or browser sessions, policy mismatch may occur.
IF retention or deletion requirements apply to shared artifacts, the pair may violate them.
mitigations: Classify data before transfer.
Keep regulated data out of B unless approved.
Set short retention on shared artifacts.
Document residency and retention boundaries.
requires-engineering: map the workflow to a formal compliance control.
